title: Doing Diagrams Is Fun, Claude Helped Me Make It More Fun
excerpt: Since college days, I’ve struggled with diagrams. I still remember my firsts UML or sequence diagrams, even though they were technically “ok,” I never managed to make them look...
html:
Doing Diagrams is fun

Since college days, I’ve struggled with diagrams. I still remember my firsts UML or sequence diagrams, even though they were technically “ok,” I never managed to make them look presentable.

That always bothered me, because diagramming is one of the most useful things an engineer can do. Turning a written spec into a visual exposes the gaps in your thinking, and it’s often the fastest way to get others to understand your solution.

Meanwhile, I’d watch coworkers open FigJam or Miro and, in a few minutes, turn an idea we’d written on paper into a near-perfect visual. The same thing took me hours.

I have always known diagramming is really two jobs. The first is technical drafting: gathering information and scoping the architecture, its components and decisions. The second is translation: turning that draft into something visual. I’m good at the first one, and I enjoy it. The second one is where I get stuck.

Why i get stuck at it?

There are different diagrams and they describe different things, from UML and sequence diagrams to frameworks like the C4 model. I have a good understanding of what to use when, but my main problems have always been three things:

  • Tools: I really like diagramming in my sketchbook, not with my trackpad. I’ve always found it tedious; at this point, I’d rather draw on my iPad lol.
  • Visuals: Sizes, fonts, arrows, alignment, etc. have always been a pain for me. Even if a diagram describes what you need it to describe, if it’s visually unbalanced or ugly, it will immediately make ANYONE reject it.
  • Audience: Most of the time, the audience for these diagrams is technical people, but I still want everyone on a team to be able to read an L1 System Context diagram and understand it. I think that’s a good rule to keep in mind.

Once I’d defined where my flaws were, they were easier to attack. And since my problems weren’t about understanding diagram frameworks or conventions, I think we know a guy who can help us with this :)

How I use Claude to help me with this

With Claude, I’ve developed a series of skills that help me with planning, developing and now, diagramming.

On my latest project, I’ve been feeding a Claude Project information about a new engagement we are kicking off: all my notes, plus the architectural decisions and assumptions made during the sales phase. That way, Claude had all the architectural context it needed. Now it was time for me to diagram the proposed architecture.

C4 Model: Similar to how I started this blog post, this is how the official C4 model site introduces itself.

The C4 model is basically a framework that sets clear levels of abstraction for a software system. That way, we can easily ask for a System Context diagram, a Container diagram and so on, and in the context of the C4 model, everyone knows what we are talking about.

This is what I usually use to describe what a project will look like and to propose an architecture, but now, with Claude, I had the chance to do it in an easy, clear way.

I instructed Claude to use the FigJam board I provided and, based on the documents I gave it, apply the C4 model to create the first two levels of abstraction: a System Context and a Container diagram. The results were simply fantastic.

Not only was Claude efficient and grounded thanks to the previous work I did, it also tackled my three main issues from above.

I didn’t have to start from scratch in FigJam, set sizes, or copy and paste boxes. Both diagrams were so clear that, so far, non-engineers have looked at them and clearly understood where we are going.

From there, my next step was to turn this into a skill I can re-run, which I’m sharing here as well :)

https://github.com/JesusGerardoAguiar/diagrams-skills

Hope you liked this short read, and if you feel the same way about diagrams, hopefully this small skill can help you out!

Happy Coding :)

title: Doing Code Review to Claude
excerpt: For some reason, I don’t wanna say I vibe coded an app, which I DIDN’T Let’s say that i had my idea and POC coded (kinda) and i wanted to start using Claude in a better way, i w...
html:
For some reason, I don’t wanna say I vibe coded an app, which I DIDN’T
Let’s say that i had my idea and POC coded (kinda) and i wanted to start using Claude in a better way, i wanted to start building stuff for me, for my own usage.

I did wanted to exercise the usage of Claude dev app like I’m using Cursor at my job, therefore i started my little thing with it, i guess right now I’m just looking for an excuse for stop paying Claude and switch to either Cursor for personal usage or Codex, i will write another blog post critizacing Claude UX experience, which i find hideous, but, their models are good i’ll give them that.

Looking for a webapp idea that combine both AI in a scalable way, that actually felt worthy of adding, Nextjs, external APIs and much more, i had this “idea” that of course is not an original one, i started building a job hunter.

Job market right now is looking like Drake Maye Super bowl game last season (ouch),

Linkedin is flooded with AI posts, X is X and in general job posts are hard to find nowadays, therefore, why not build a simple app which uses public APIs (wework remontly, himalayas, others), creates a pipeline, use Antropic API with my profile and from that pipeline, it selects the jobs that matches my skills, preferences and so on, but let’s not stop there, it can also help me tailor my cover letter, CV, and also, track the progress of the application.

Of course not everything on that process is AI hands-on, for example, reaching out to the recruiter is on my end, or, moving the application to the proper status (which probably will be ghosted lol).

So yes, I find it as a good mid-size project on which i can play with it, see more and more of Claude capabilities, not to use it as a real job hunter, but good as a POC at the end of the day.

Well, i started working with Claude on this, Sonnet 5 and let’s get rolling with it.

After multiple PRs, deploying, hosting with Vercel and token resets, bugs etc i think we landed in a pretty decent MVP, which i was very happy about, at the end, we worked it out. I even told Claude to use PostHog design as a reference since i love that 90's windows nostalgia that PostHog uses.

But the reason why i’m writing this post is because, i one of the PRs Claude did, while reviewing it, i said “this code is s***”.

I’m still the same guy that years ago, wrote this blog post , so you know me, im picky af about the code.

Currently at my company, i give extensive code reviews, i honestly deeply care about the state of the codebase, even if AI will be the main one coding on it, i don’t care, code is code and it needs to be well written but most importantly, it needs to make sense.

i stumbled across code like this

Yea, it is trying to add a “S” at the of “application” if total is greater than 1.

Again, i know what you are thinking “Jesus, are you being serious?”

Hell yea i am, Claude could’ve created a function that pluralizes any word, and take it outside of the JSX and not use that hideus inline rendering.

There are other way more important cases, for example, see over here

Oh yea, i can see a lot that we can refactor

  • Query state logic being manually managed.
  • fetching logic being used directly on the onSubmit instead of using an API utility function for a cleaner “fetchApplication” function.
  • Multiple useStates, instead of using useReducer or a single consilidated state const [formData, setFormData] = useState(…).

And there are others like Inputs lack standard accessibility and browser auto-fill attributes like required, autoComplete, and aria-invalid .

But honestly, the ones that caught my attention more are on the API utility and useStates, i believe any senior DEV will consider these good patterns, so why don’t Claude agents consider it?, is the pattern just to write as fast as it can? and consume the most amount of tokens on doing so?

The codebase is flooded of cases like these, which drives me to the conclusion: Yes, ma guy can code, but at what scale? Unless I spent an enomours time adding skills to it, rules and multiple .md files explaining how i want it to code, his code probably will be a spaghetti or an unpatterned code.

Planning is the key to all of it, last year, my team completed a BIG consolidation of stacks and codebases which took us in total, 10 months of work. We started in August 2024, the first 2–3 months we spent on planning, planning every single detail, the patterns, the folder structure, the libraries, the naming variables and so on.

That codebase is complex but simple at the same time, it can be read like a book, and that’s because of it’s foundations. This webapp I made, i will probably discard it, I won’t be using it all the time, so not much to discuss, but, how many systems right now are out there that are being used by people that had 0 review on foundations and it was almost 100% coded via AI? I think that’s kinda of a ticking bomb, so it’s better to have engineers to help the AI refactor and guide it accordingly, which again, I think AI with the proper amount of time and collaboration, it’s HUGE advantage, after the cellphone the biggest invention of our timeline.

Hopefully you guys liked this one!, I’m back at the rodeo of writing, i want to connect with this again :)

PS: this blog post was fully written by a me, a human, AI was used to review grammar since English is not my primary language 👉🏼👈🏼

title: Why useState is out of date
excerpt: A few weeks ago, I wrote a post criticizing useState, which you can read more about here. Now, I have a new perspective on why useState will eventually become a hook that we sto...
html:
A few weeks ago, I wrote a post criticizing useState, which you can read more about here. Now, I have a new perspective on why useState will eventually become a hook that we stop using.

You may ask why we use useState in the first place. Well, it’s a way to add state to a React component, which means we can define a variable and have our component “change” to it when it updates or re-renders, as we call it in React. Take this counter component, for example:

The counter component is simple, defining a state variable counter that changes every time we click the "increase" button. It's a small piece of code, so the performance issue with every update re-rendering the entire component isn't noticeable. But imagine if we had larger components with multiple variables defined like the message variable I mentioned earlier. Every time the counter changes, the message variable gets redefined, which can lead to performance issues we want to avoid.

useSignal: Our hero

This is where useSignal comes in. useSignal is a hook from Qwik, which you may have heard of from Preact. To put it briefly, useSignal is similar to useState but with a more focused approach. Let me explain.

useSignal takes advantage of something I really like — in order to get and set a new value of count, you access it the same way using the value property of the signal. Since useSignal also takes advantage of reactivity, it only changes the parts of the component where count.value is being read.

Here’s an image from the creator of qwik, which he uses to compare code using useState and useSignal (you can follow him on Twitter @mhevery).

Both examples are similar to the one above. As you can see, on the right side, every time setCount is executed, the whole component re-renders. On the left side, it only changes where we use the count.value. This is a clean and fast solution.

In conclusion, I hope that at some point in the future, we will have a native implementation of useSignals in React. It’s an extremely powerful and useful tool for cases where you want to keep your code clean and have a component that performs well over time.

thanks for reading me and happy coding :)

html:
3 Tips for Optimizing
Svelte Performance

Svelte is well-known for its high performance, but there are several best practices you should employ to guarantee your Svelte applications run as quickly as possible. In this post, we’ll look at various tips and strategies for improving Svelte performance, along with some code examples.

These strategies are frontend agonistic, which means they may be used to other frontend technologies such as React or Vue.

1. Use Code Splitting

Code splitting is one of the most effective techniques to boost the performance of your Svelte apps. Instead of loading everything at once, divide your code into smaller portions that can be loaded on demand. Here’s an example of code splitting in action with Svelte:

This code dynamically imports the MyComponent Svelte component when it is needed. This can help reduce the initial load time of your application and improve the user experience.

2. Lazy Load Images

Images can be a significant impediment for online speed, particularly on mobile devices. Lazy loading images, which means loading them only when they are needed, is one technique to optimize picture performance. Here’s an example of sluggish image loading in Svelte:

In this code, the data-src attribute is used to specify the URL of the actual image, while the loading="lazy" attribute tells the browser to only load the image when it's in the viewport.

3. Use Virtual Lists for Large Data Sets

When dealing with a huge data collection that needs to be presented in a list, performance can quickly become a bottleneck. Rendering all of the items in the list, even if they are not now visible, will slow down and sluggish your application. One solution is to use virtual lists, which only display the items that are currently visible on the screen.

In this example, we’re using svelte-virtual-list to render a virtual list of items. We're specifying the itemHeight and the height of the list to determine the size of the virtual container. We're also passing in a renderItem function that is responsible for rendering each item in the list.

By using a third-party library like svelte-virtual-list, you can implement virtual lists in your Svelte applications and improve their performance when dealing with large data sets.

These are just a few examples of ways you can optimize Svelte performance. By following these best practices and experimenting with other performance tweaks, you can build blazing-fast Svelte applications that deliver an excellent user experience.

Happy coding :)

title: We all take notes, but not everyone takes them in the most efficient way.
excerpt: We all take notes, but not everyone takes them in the most efficient way.
html:
We all take notes, but not everyone takes them in the most efficient way.

In today’s post, we will discuss a 4-step technique for taking notes as efficiently as possible.

This method is called: The CCCC Technique — Consume, Collect, Connect, and Create.

1.- “You are what you consume”: The information our brain retains is like food for our body. It’s likely that if we have a balanced and nutritious diet, we’ll feel better and healthier than if we eat processed food. The same goes for information. On the internet, we are constantly bombarded with information that is not useful to us, which distracts us from the information we want to read and retain. So if we want to take better notes, we need to regulate what we consume.

In my case, I use my Instagram to view posts about inspiration, from websites, design, fashion, and productivity. And I’ll let you in on a secret: I have 90% of my friends muted, haha.

Once you can filter the information you want to consume, it’s time to collect it.

2.- Collecting everything in one place is your goal. It’s worst if we use different ways to take notes, whether they’re text or digital, as it will be very difficult to locate what you want to revisit to read. Loose notes are our enemies; they waste our time and we can’t connect back to our notes. For my part, I’m a very digital person and take notes digitally, and beyond which app I use, I think the most useful tool I have is “CMD+F” for those who have a Mac or “CTRL + F” in Windows to find the phrase or text I want to read.

3.- Start connecting your ideas.

Your ideas are the sum of what you have consumed in the past. When sleeping or being bored, your brain creates connections between all the ideas. For too long, people have classified their notes into folders or using labels. While it seems to make sense on paper, this process prevents you from making meaningful connections and generating great ideas. This is why labels and folders don’t work. If you’re looking to generate creative ideas, find new solutions, and stand out, you want to mimic the way your brain generates ideas and transplant them into your note-taking system. Enter: backlinks. Backlinks are how you connect your notes to each other. It’s the next generation of effective note-taking. To create great backlinks, simply ask yourself a question: What does the note I just took remind me of? Link the corresponding note. Done.

4.- Create value for others.

Ideas are meant to be shared.

If you’re like us, you love discovering and sharing knowledge, as the saying goes “Money grows by saving it, but knowledge grows by sharing it.” That’s why, thanks to the other 3 steps, you can create value from all notes and ideas, it will help you better retain information and have better conclusions with your ideas.

For this, I use 2 apps which I’ll talk more about at the end of this mini-series.

And you, how do you keep your notes and ideas?

title: Bundlr + Arweave + NextJS: Permanent and Decentralized Storage
excerpt: Blockchain technology has had a major impact on data storage and access. Arweave, a decentralized data storage platform built on blockchain, offers a secure and permanent soluti...
html:
Blockchain technology has had a major impact on data storage and access. Arweave, a decentralized data storage platform built on blockchain, offers a secure and permanent solution for storing digital assets such as images, PDFs, and websites.

Arweave utilizes a wallet and token system for uploading data to its permanent storage, which is designed to be more robust than IPFS’s caching mechanism. However, the requirement of using an Arweave wallet may limit its user base, as many individuals in the web3 space prefer to choose their own wallet depending on the blockchain it’s built on.

Thankfully, we have a solution for that:

Introducing Bundlr Protocol

Bundlr is a protocol or, as some refer to it, an adapter for Arweave. It enables you to connect any blockchain of your choice, whether it be a Layer 1 or Layer 2 blockchain such as Solana, Polygon, or Ethereum, with any token you desire, whether it be native or non-native. With Bundlr, you no longer have to worry about limiting your user base by requiring them to use an Arweave wallet.

Thanks to its JavaScript library, developers can easily upload data to Arweave without needing an Arweave wallet, making it more accessible and user-friendly for a wider range of individuals.

How Does it Work?

Bundlr operates based on an architecture that allows users create a “Bundlr node” associated to their wallet address. In this Node users can transfer their funds from their existing wallet (such as MetaMask or Phantom) to their Bundlr Node before they can start using it.

With this, you can tell Bundlr to expect funds from a blockchain and the token you want and will also persist the user wallet address in order to fetch it funds in the future.

Let’s start coding

I did a small code example with Nextjs (I’m using Next 12)

import { WebBundlr } from "@bundlr-network/client";
import { useState, useEffect, useRef } from "react";

function MyApp({ Component, pageProps }) {
  const [bundlrInstance, setBundlrInstance] = useState();
  const [balance, setBalance] = useState(0);
  const bundlrRef = useRef();

  useEffect(() => {
    initialiseBundlr();
  }, []);

  async function initialiseBundlr() {
    await ethereum.request({ method: "eth_accounts" });
    const provider = new providers.Web3Provider(window.ethereum);
    await provider._ready();
    /* here i can choose to use the blockchain I need, 
it can be a devnet or a mainnet */
    const bundlr = new WebBundlr(
      "<https://devnet.bundlr.network>",
      "matic",
      provider,
      { providerUrl: "<https://matic-mumbai.chainstacklabs.com>" }
    );
    await bundlr.ready();
    setBundlrInstance(bundlr);
    bundlrRef.current = bundlr;
    fetchBalance();
  }

  async function fetchBalance() {
    const bal = await bundlrRef.current.getLoadedBalance();
    console.log("bal: ", utils.formatEther(bal.toString()));
    setBalance(utils.formatEther(bal.toString()));
  }

  return <Component {...pageProps} />;
}
export default MyApp;

In this example, I created a new Bundlr instance; this instance, or node, will be used to process transactions on the Bundlr network.

You can see that after I create the Bundlr Instance, I fetch the balance, but you might be thinking “But we are creating a new instance”, and you’d be right. Bundlr linked your wallet to the Node when creating the Bundlr instance, so every time you “create” a new node, Bundlr looks for any Node that has your wallet address linked and uses that one.

Funding a Node

For funding a Node, we gotta tweak a little bit our _app.js to pass the bundlrInstance through child components, for this, i will use React Context just to keep it simple

import { WebBundlr } from "@bundlr-network/client";
import { useState, useEffect, useRef } from "react";
import { MainContext } from "context";

function MyApp({ Component, pageProps }) {
  const [bundlrInstance, setBundlrInstance] = useState();
  const [balance, setBalance] = useState(0);
  const bundlrRef = useRef();
  useEffect(() => {
    initialiseBundlr();
  }, []);

async function initialiseBundlr() {
    await ethereum.request({ method: "eth_accounts" });
    const provider = new providers.Web3Provider(window.ethereum);
    await provider._ready();
    const bundlr = new WebBundlr(
      "<https://devnet.bundlr.network>",
      "matic",
      provider,
      { providerUrl: "<https://matic-mumbai.chainstacklabs.com>" }
    );
    await bundlr.ready();
    setBundlrInstance(bundlr);
    bundlrRef.current = bundlr;
    fetchBalance();
  }

  async function fetchBalance() {
    const bal = await bundlrRef.current.getLoadedBalance();
    console.log("bal: ", utils.formatEther(bal.toString()));
    setBalance(utils.formatEther(bal.toString()));
  }

  return (
    <MainContext.Provider
      value={{
        initialiseBundlr,
        bundlrInstance,
        balance,
        fetchBalance,
      }}
    >
      <Component {...pageProps} />
    </MainContext.Provider>
  );
}

export default MyApp;

We this, We can now create our Fund component

import { useState, useContext, useEffect } from "react";
import BigNumber from 'bignumber.js'
import { MainContext } from "context";

const Funds = () => {
  const { balance, bundlrInstance, fetchBalance } = useContext(MainContext);
  const [amount, setAmount] = useState()

  function parseInput (input) {
    const conv = new BigNumber(input).multipliedBy(bundlrInstance.currencyConfig.base[1])
    if (conv.isLessThan(1)) {
      console.log('error: value too small')
      return
    } else {
      return conv
    }
  }

  async function fundWallet() {
    if (!amount) return
    const amountParsed = parseInput(amount)
    try {
      await bundlrInstance.fund(amountParsed)
      fetchBalance()
    } catch (err) {
      console.log('Error funding wallet: ', err)
    }
  }

  useEffect(() => {
    fetchBalance()
  }, [balance])

  return (
    <div>
      <div>
        <p>Total Balance</p>
        <h3>{Math.round(balance * 100) / 100} MATIC</h3>
      </div>
      
      <div>
        <p>Fund Wallet</p>
        <input
          placeholder="amount"
          className={`text-primary ${inputStyle}`}
          onChange={(e) => setAmount(e.target.value)}
        />
        <button onClick={fundWallet}>
          Send transaction
        </button>
      </div>
    </div>
  );
};

export default Funds;

As you can see on fundWallet() We first need to parse the amount We want to fund to BigNumber, and to do a proper conversion, we gotta use the currencyConfig by bundlerInstance

As simple as it is, you can now use those funds to upload a file to Arweave through Bundlr, let’s get that done!

For uploading a file, We need to first calculate the cost of the file, for this, Bundlr has a function getPrice(bytes) that expects the file size in bytes, this will give if a cost in BigNumber, the function will look a little bit like this:

async function checkUploadCost(bytes) {
    if (bytes && bundlrInstance) {
      const cost = await bundlrInstance.getPrice(bytes);
      const formattedCost = utils.formatEther(cost.toString());
      setFileCost(formattedCost);
    }
 }

Notice that, i’m only parsing the cost for showing it to the user, but getPrice will return the price in the currency you set when you create the Bundlr instance.

So let’s wrap up our upload file component:

import { useState, useContext, useEffect } from "react";
import { MainContext } from "context";
import { utils } from "ethers";
import Funds from "../components/Funds";

export default function UploadFile() {
  const { bundlrInstance } = useContext(MainContext);
  const [file, setFile] = useState();
  const [localVideo, setLocalVideo] = useState();
  const [fileCost, setFileCost] = useState();
  const [fileSize, setFileSize] = useState(0);
  const [URI, setURI] = useState();

  function onFileChange(e) {
    const file = e.target.files[0];
    if (!file) return;
    setFileSize(file.size);
    if (file) {
      const video = URL.createObjectURL(file);
      setLocalVideo(video);
      let reader = new FileReader();
      reader.onload = function (e) {
        if (reader.result) {
          setFile(Buffer.from(reader.result));
        }
      };
      reader.readAsArrayBuffer(file);
    }
  }

  useEffect(() => {
    checkUploadCost(fileSize);
  }, [fileSize]);

  async function checkUploadCost(bytes) {
    if (bytes && bundlrInstance) {
      const cost = await bundlrInstance.getPrice(bytes);
      const formattedCost = utils.formatEther(cost.toString());
      setFileCost(formattedCost);
    }
  }

  async function saveVideo() {
    const tags = [{ name: "Content-Type", value: "text/plain" }];
    const videoTags = [{ name: "Content-Type", value: "video/mp4" }];
    try {
      let txVideo = await bundlrInstance.uploader.upload(file, videoTags);
      try {
        setURI(`http://arweave.net/${txVideo.data.id}`);
      } catch (err) {
        console.log("error uploading video with metadata: ", err);
      }
    } catch (err) {
      console.log("Error uploading video: ", err);
    }
  }

  return (
    <div>
      <div>
        <p>Add Video</p>
        <div>
          <input type="file" onChange={onFileChange} />
        </div>
       
     
        {localVideo && (
          <video key={localVideo} width="520" controls className={videoStyle}>
            <source src={localVideo} type="video/mp4" />
          </video>
        )}
        {fileCost && (
          <h4>Cost to upload: {Math.round(fileCost * 1000) / 1000} MATIC</h4>
        )}
        {URI && (
          <div>
            <p>
              <a href={URI}>{URI}</a>
            </p>
          </div>
        )}
       
            <button onClick={saveVideo}>
              Save Video
            </button>
         
      </div>
      <Funds />
    </div>
  );
}

Ok, this is a BIG component, most of it is just input components and handlers, which isn’t a big deal, but I want to focus on saveVideo()

This function does exactly what it says it does: it saves the video to Arweave. To do so, we must utilize the upload() function from the bundlrInstance. As the name implies, it uploads the file to Arweave via Bundlr and returns the file's id in Arweave, as simple as that, and then we simply generate the url using that id and that's it! We successfully uploaded a file to long-term storage.

Take that, AWS! 🎉🎉🎉

Conclusion

In conclusion, the Bundlr protocol and the Arweave network offer numerous benefits to users who are looking for a decentralized and permanent solution for data storage. With Bundlr, users are no longer limited by the requirement of using an Arweave wallet, making it easier and more accessible to a wider range of individuals.

Furthermore, the permanent and decentralized nature of Arweave provides the added benefit of protecting users’ data from censorship and government interference, ensuring that their digital assets are safe and secure for years to come. In an era where privacy and security are becoming increasingly important, the Bundlr protocol and Arweave network provide a valuable solution for those looking to store and protect their digital assets.

Happy coding :)

title: Taming the useState Hell: An Introduction to useReducer in React
excerpt: I was working on my most recent project, a platform for scheduling decentralized streamings, and as the name “schedule” implies, you have to enter dates, titles, amount of parti...
html:
I was working on my most recent project, a platform for scheduling decentralized streamings, and as the name “schedule” implies, you have to enter dates, titles, amount of participants, and so much more.

So I created my component for this form, let’s call it “ScheduleForm,” and of course the question “how am I going to manage the state of this form” emerged. The answer was simple, because it was only local state, I used useState, but I ended up with something like this.

But this code made me think.

“How can I tell whether the end date is before the start date?”

“How can I know if my title is too long?”

“Do I need to write a function for each form checker? “How can I handle errors?”

Sure, we could hold our breath and hope that everytime we call set*() we would remember (or even know) to validate all of these things before writing to state, but I don't sleep well knowing that things are just sitting in such an easily broken state.

Of course, the code above has an obvious refactor.

but sadly, it has the same problems, just lesser code

Here’s where the useReducer comes into play

useReducer It’s a more complex method of handling state in React that’s a powerful alternative to useState. The useReducer hook accepts two arguments: a reducer function and a starting state. The reducer function takes the current state and an action as input and outputs a new state. This allows for the clean and systematic management of complicated state changes and interactions between various state variables.

So, the code above can be refactored as follows:

You may be thinking, “Jesus, this is still the same as the code above,” and you are correct in one aspect.

You see, while the above format hopes that you always remember to spread on ...scheduleValues so you don't mess up by mutating the object directly (causing React to not re-render as expected), it still misses out on the most important benefit of useReducer which is the ability to supply a function that controls state transitions.

Returning to ‘useReducer,’ the only difference is that you get an extra argument, which is a function that can assist us ensure that each state transition is safe and valid:

This has the big advantage of ensuring that your state is always valid in a fully centralized manner.

So, even if additional code is introduced in the future, and future developers on your team call updateEvent() with potentially erroneous data, your callback will always trigger.

For example, we may wish to always ensure that the end date is never before the start date (since this would be illogical), and that the title has a maximum length of 100 characters:

Having this function makes a HUGE difference when you need to validate data, handle errors and making everything cleaner and more scalable through time since prevent direct mutation of state.

When should i use which

The choice between useState and useReducer depends on the complexity of your state management and the size of your application.

useState is best suited for managing simple state values, such as toggle switches, input fields, or counter values. If your state management only involves a few values that are simple to update and don't have complex interactions with each other, useState is a great choice.

useReducer, on the other hand, is best suited for more complex state management, such as data management, form submissions, or large-scale state updates. If your state management involves multiple state values that have complex interactions with each other, or if your application is growing in size and complexity, it may be a good idea to use useReducer.

It’s also worth noting that you can use both useState and useReducer in the same application. For example, you can use useState to manage simple state values, while using useReducer to manage complex state interactions between multiple state values.

In general, useState is a great starting point for state management in React, but as your application grows, you may find that useReducer provides a better solution for managing complex state.

This is just short intro to useReducer world, than im planning to expand a future post :)

title: Redux Toolkit Query and React Query: Which should I use when?
excerpt: First and foremost, let me state that this is not a one-on-one comparison, nor is it a “which one is better” debate. This is an article on two libraries that are highly powerful...
html:
First and foremost, let me state that this is not a one-on-one comparison, nor is it a “which one is better” debate. This is an article on two libraries that are highly powerful, comparing them in different circumstances and discussing the merits that both have.

Lets start 🙂

Redux Toolkit Query and React Query are two popular libraries for managing and fetching data in React applications. Both libraries aim to make it easy to handle data in a scalable and maintainable way, but they approach this problem in slightly different ways.

Redux Toolkit Query is built on top of Redux, the popular state management library. It provides a set of utilities for defining and managing data in the Redux store, as well as handling fetching and caching of data. The main advantage of using Redux Toolkit Query is that it fits seamlessly into the existing Redux architecture and allows you to use the powerful dev tools and middleware that are available for Redux. This can be especially useful if you are already using Redux in your application and want to keep all of your state in one place.

React Query, on the other hand, is a standalone library that is not tied to any specific state management library. It focuses on providing a simple API for fetching and caching data, and it can be used in any React application regardless of whether it uses Redux or another state management library. The main advantage of React Query is its simplicity and flexibility. It is easy to get started with and it provides a lot of built-in features such as automatic caching and stale-while-revalidate.

How do they work?

RTKQuery has a syntax that is quite similar to React Query, however there are a few differences in how everything is put up.

You must first define the endpoints you will need for querying and mutating data, which you can do using the utility function createApi. You can also define the baseQuery that you will use for your endpoints, which by default uses Fetch and will handle errors and resolving data, but you can edit this and provide your own fetchBaseQuery, which we will leave as default for now.

You can also define the query function for each endpoint, where you can provide the url, method, params, and much more.

As a result, you’ll have something like this.

Furthermore, createApi will use autogenerate hooks for the execution of your endpoints, which is where RTKQuery and React Query begin to resemble one other, because React Query employs hooks for handling Query and Mutation actions, but we’ll get to that later.

When you have your hooks, you can use them in this manner.

Or mutate data like this

Of course the createApi and it’s hooks has more params to use, like cache functionalities, re-fetch queries on every specific amount time, and other stuff that you can read more about here

The React Query on the other hand, the main advantage of React Query is its simplicity and flexibility. Unlike RTKQuery, which is limited to what we define in the createApi function, React Query allows you to define your own query/mutation on the fly. However, you must still define how you want each query to be executed (via fetch, axios, etc.) and how you will handle errors.

But, what is fetchPosts? It’s a Query Function, which can be literally any function that returns a promise. The promise that is returned should either resolve the data or throw an error

So you will have something like this:

And we can clean this up a little bit like this

Same logic applies to Mutation data, the hook useMutation will provide you with a trigger function, and in the Query Function, you can define what to do with that data.

Of course useQuery and useMutation hooks has more params to use, like cache functionalities, re-fetch queries on every specific amount time, and other stuff that you can read more about here

Caching

Caching data in React Query works by saving the data in memory and using it for subsequent requests instead of sending a new request to the server. This improves performance by lowering the number of network queries and the time required to obtain the data. React Query also has cache management functionality such as invalidating stale data and addressing network failures.

Caching data in Redux Toolkit Query works similarly to React Query, except it uses the Redux store to manage the cache. This means that the cached data is saved in the store and may be retrieved and updated by the application’s various components. The Redux store also enables simple cache management, such as invalidating stale data and resolving network problems. Furthermore, Redux Toolkit Query includes a collection of actions and selectors for dealing with the cache, allowing for more fine-grained control over how data is saved and retrieved.

Which should I use when?

Keeping in simple, you can use whatever the F**** you want, both are great, both perform great but, since the aim of this post is write about best scenarios to use them, lets dig a little bit about it

When picking between React Query and Redux Toolkit Query, keep the following aspects in mind:

  • Application complexity: If your application is simple and does not require a lot of global state management, React Query might be a better choice because it is primarily focused on handling data requests and caching. If your application is more complicated and requires a centralized store for handling state, Redux Toolkit Query, which connects with the Redux store, may be a better option.
  • Team familiarity: If your team is already familiar with React Query and are comfortable with its API, it may be easier to continue using it. Similarly, if your team is already familiar with Redux and are comfortable with the Redux ecosystem, Redux Toolkit Query may be a better fit.

The one I care about the most is complexity and scalability over time, and I’m not going to lie, I prefer to specify everything in one place and then export and utilize it.

CreateApi is stupid powerful, but if the endpoint has some logic that you can’t execute with createApi, you have to use createAsyncThunk, which is beyond the parameters of createApi, which complicates things a little.

As a result, when you think about it, React Query covers all “scenarios” for querying and altering data, regardless of whether the logic is sophisticated or not, and even if there is a third party in between, the way of doing things will remain consistent, which is also strong thought time.

Conclusion

Finally, Redux Toolkit Query and React Query are also popular tools for maintaining and retrieving data in React applications. They both want to make it simple to handle data in a scalable and maintainable manner, but they go about it in slightly different ways.

Both have advantages and disadvantages, and it is vital to consider them while deciding which to utilize.

It is critical that engineers do not utilize libraries solely because everyone else is doing so. Instead, explore first, compare them, and choose which one best meets your needs.

Thanks for reading me 🙂

title: Achieve great performance with this easy takes in React
excerpt: Building large and complex react applications may lead us to pay attention to some details than other, for example, trying to implement l ow coupling solutions in order to gain...
html:
Building large and complex react applications may lead us to pay attention to some details than other, for example, trying to implement low coupling solutions in order to gain more maintainability in the future is one of the hardest things to achieve and we put a lot of effort and thought into it, but, for performance must of the time is something that we don’t have in our mind all the time.

The reality here is having an React app with good performance maybe easy to achieve if we consider using the small techniques since the start, but, if we try to refactor all of these at the end can be a really pain in the a**

That’s why I encourage you to keep these in mind when you are going to implement a new feature into your React app:

  • Importing lazy loading components or Code-Splitting:

Most React apps will have their files “bundled” using tools like Webpack, Rollup or Browserify. Bundling is the process of following imported files and merging them into a single file: a “bundle”. This bundle can then be included on a webpage to load an entire app at once.

When We use React, most of the time our files will be bundled with tools like webpack or vite, as our app grows, so will our bundle and if we import everything at once, our app will take ages to load, that’s why We use techniques like code-splitting. Doing this in your app can help you “lazy-load” just the things that are currently needed by the user, which can dramatically improve the performance of your app.

Sometimes, i tent to use React Lazy for lazy-loading routes, and, inside of those routes, i also lazy loads components that i don’t care if they are loaded at last.

Here for example, the first components that the user will see and interact first are not lazy loaded because i want them to be loaded as fast as it can, and the component that the user will interact the least are lazy loaded.

  • Using webp format for images

WebP is a modern image format that provides superior lossless and lossy compression for images on the web. Using WebP, webmasters and web developers can create smaller, richer images that make the web faster.

  • Rendering lists with Object.keys

In React, you can use the Object.keys() method to get an array of the keys in an object, which you can then use to render a list. Here's an example of how you could use it:

This would render a list like this:

Using Object.keys() to get an array of the keys in an object can be an optimal way to render a list of items in React because it allows you to use the built-in Array.prototype.map() method to create a new array of elements by iterating over the array of keys and creating a list item element for each key.

This can be more efficient than other approaches, such as using a for loop or for...in loop to iterate over the keys in the object and create the list items. It's also easier to read and write, since it uses functional programming constructs that are built into JavaScript.

Additionally, using the key prop in the list items allows React to optimize the rendering of the list by keeping track of which items have changed, added, or removed, rather than re-rendering the entire list whenever there is a change. This can improve the performance of your app, especially if the list is large or updates frequently.

  • Use React Suspense

React Suspense is a new feature in React that makes it easier to manage the loading state of asynchronous data in your application. It allows you to “suspend” the rendering of a component tree until a certain condition is met, and display a fallback UI in the meantime.

Using React Suspense can be optimal because it allows you to declaratively specify the loading behavior of your application, rather than having to manually manage it through props and state. This can make your code easier to understand and maintain, since the loading logic is isolated in a single place rather than scattered throughout your components.

Additionally, React Suspense can improve the performance of your application by allowing you to load data in parallel and by avoiding the need to render intermediate loading states. This can result in a better user experience, especially on slow networks or devices.

Overall, React Suspense can help you build more efficient and user-friendly applications by making it easier to manage the loading state of asynchronous data.

  • Use React Memo

useMemo is a hook in React that allows you to memoize the value of a function component. This means that the component will only be re-rendered if one of the dependencies has changed.

Using useMemo can be optimal in situations where the component has expensive calculations that do not need to be performed on every render, such as when rendering a large list or when making expensive API calls. By memoizing the value of the component, you can avoid unnecessary re-renders and improve the performance of your application.
